summary:
Cesar operates under Colombia's national legal framework, and no Cesar-specific finding on trans law, enforcement practice or incidents is available for this department. The rules a trans visitor faces in Cesar are the national ones.

Legal gender recognition is a notarial process with no surgery or court ruling required, and applies equally in Cesar. Since 1993 a person may change the gender marker on a Colombian birth certificate; current options are F, M, NB (no binario) and T (transgénero). On 9 July 2026 outgoing justice minister Jorge Iván Cuervo signed Decree 0732 of 2026, which obliges public notaries to complete the request within five business days, makes the first request (and a simultaneous name change) free of charge, and shields the change history from public disclosure. The Constitutional Court's 4 February 2022 ruling ordered the government to offer the nonbinary option to everyone and to ask Congress to amend the relevant laws, and since August 2023 passports issued within Colombia offer three gender options: male, female and X.

Bureaucratic obstruction has been documented. A 2016 report, Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia, by OutRight Action International, El Aquelarre Trans and PAIIS, documented notaries refusing to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity.

Violence against trans Colombians is documented at national scale, though no Cesar-specific incident appears in the sources. The Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 reports 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024, and records an activist's statement that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording the killings as ordinary cases. A CNN article of 6 August 2025 reports a wave of attacks on LGBTQ+ people across Colombia following the killing of Sara Millerey.
tangentialFactors:
The Guardian investigation of 30 July 2024 documents armed groups in Caquetá giving trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed and circulating 'social cleansing' flyers against trans women. Caquetá is a separate department; no comparable armed-group campaign is documented for Cesar in these sources.

The prosecutor's office's failure to recognise transfemicide, as reported by an activist quoted in the same investigation, means killings of trans women may be recorded in ways that obscure the pattern of targeting, a risk that applies nationally including in Cesar.
localsOnly:
Colombian birth-certificate gender-marker changes are a notarial process available to residents as well as visitors, and Decree 0732 of 2026 imposes a five-business-day completion deadline on public notaries, waives the fee for a first request and a simultaneous name change, and shields the change history from public disclosure.

The 2016 Cartografía de derechos trans en Colombia report found that notaries had refused to process name changes and recommended ending the psychiatric pathologisation of transgender identity, indicating that formal entitlements have not always been honoured at the counter.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Cesar-specific source was available in this inventory. Whether Decree 0732 of 2026 and the Constitutional Court's nonbinary ruling have been implemented by notaries in Cesar specifically is not sourced here, as is any local enforcement record on hate-crime or transfemicide handling in the department.

The inventory does not resolve whether the national statistics on trans killings include any cases in Cesar, nor whether armed-group 'social cleansing' campaigns of the kind documented in Caquetá and Guajira operate in this department.
